absent: Virtual filesystem status lookup internals and permission checks beyond the call boundary.
Security hook decision logic for filesystem status queries.
Filesystem specific statfs provider contracts and error ranges.
Filename lookup, automount and stale handle revalidation mechanics.
User namespace identifier mapping edge cases and overflow handling.
Superblock lock implementation and lifecycle state transitions beyond born dying dead.
Pressure ratio adjustment and list LRU shrink accounting.
Exact numeric values of mount, superblock and status flag constants.
Compatibility structure layouts and width thresholds across architectures.
Writeback unregister and retired state effects on later lookups.

findings.text: Path based extended status query validates caller requested field set and synchronization mode, removes a kernel only change cookie request, obtains internal status through the virtual filesystem layer, then formats the result into caller memory and propagates lookup or copy failures.

Descriptor based extended status query applies the same field set and mode checks and kernel only request filtering as the path variant, then queries status by open descriptor and renders to caller memory.
A request is rejected as invalid when any reserved field bit is set or when the synchronization mode selects both available sync behaviors at once.

The internal to user extended status conversion starts from zeroed memory, hides kernel only result and attribute indicators from the exposed mask, translates ownership into the caller user namespace with munged fallback, splits device identities into major and minor parts, and copies times, sizes, identifiers and alignment and subvolume related attributes.

The extended status system entry resolves an optional pathname and, when no name is present with a non negative directory descriptor, delegates to the descriptor helper with automount suppressed; otherwise it delegates to the pathname helper with original flags.

Compatibility status formatting fails with an overflow error when a narrow device, inode number, link count or non large file size field cannot represent the internal value, and fails with a fault error when the final user copy cannot complete.

Compatibility wrappers for classic status, link status, directory relative status and descriptor status each fetch internal status through the corresponding virtual filesystem helper and then format through a shared compatibility copier, returning the first error encountered.

Byte count updates that adjust block and remainder counters are serialized by a per inode spin lock in the safe wrappers, while the unlocked arithmetic helpers and the direct setter require the caller to already hold that lock.

Byte accounting treats storage in units of five hundred twelve bytes, carrying excess remainder into the block counter on addition and borrowing from the block counter when the remainder underflows on subtraction; the setter derives both counters by splitting the absolute total.
Device association record holds five members: sd_dev for identity, sd_sb for owning superblock, sd_ref for pin counting, sd_node for hash linkage, sd_rcu for deferred reclamation.
The device table is a resizable hash keyed by device identity, configured with key length and offsets locating the key field and the linkage field inside the association record.

Device table walks acquire read side critical section protection while attempting to gain a stable pin on each entry, release the critical section before returning, and drop the previous pin after advancing to the next entry.

Superblock lookup by device iterates colliding table entries, skips instances whose super lock cannot be acquired, takes an additional passive reference on the first lockable match, releases the table pin and returns the locked superblock, or returns null when no entry matches.

Mount option state is projected into the filesystem status flag word so that read only, execution, device, identifier, timing and symlink following restrictions each set a corresponding reporting bit.
Superblock option state contributes synchronous, mandatory locking and read only reporting bits, and the combined mount and superblock projection always includes a validity marker.

Internal filesystem status query requires a filesystem supplied operation, clears the destination, applies a security check that can veto the call, invokes the provider, and substitutes block size for fragment size when the provider leaves the latter zero.
Path based status adds computed mount flags after a successful dentry query, while the filesystem identifier helper performs an internal query on a dentry and extracts only the identifier field.
Pathname filesystem status starts with follow and automount lookup, queries the resolved path, releases the reference, and on a stale handle indication retries with revalidation requested.
Descriptor filesystem status validates that the descriptor refers to an open file and then queries status through the file path, failing with a bad descriptor error when empty.

Native and compatibility filesystem status renderers start from zeroed memory when layouts differ and fail with overflow when block counts, sizes or file counts exceed the narrowed user field width, tolerating an all ones sentinel for unknown file counts in the narrow case.
Sized filesystem status variants reject callers whose size argument differs from the expected user structure size.
Native pathname and descriptor filesystem status entries fetch internal status and then render through native sized copiers, with sixty four bit forms enforcing an exact size match.

Compatibility pathname and descriptor filesystem status entries share the same lookup helpers as native forms but render through compatibility copiers, with sixty four bit compatibility forms delegating to kernel helpers that enforce size matching.

Legacy device status resolves a superblock from an encoded device number, queries its root, drops the superblock reference, and returns only free block and free inode counts in a zeroed user structure, clamping the inode count on some thirty two bit builds.

Superblock instance list protection uses a dedicated spin lock, while lifetime and teardown use shared versus exclusive super locks; the two drop helpers each pair the matching unlock with a reference release.

Reclaim scanning of a superblock refuses work when the reclaim context forbids filesystem activity or the shared super lock is unavailable, then divides the requested scan count proportionally among directory, inode and filesystem object populations, always making minimal progress and pruning directories before inodes before filesystem caches.

Reclaim object counting avoids acquiring the shared super lock for scalability, reports empty until the born state is visible across a read barrier, and otherwise sums directory, inode and filesystem populations with pressure adjustment.
Retirement asserts block device backing, takes the exclusive super lock, unregisters per superblock writeback state when present, marks the instance retired, and releases the exclusive lock.

Iteration over superblocks of a filesystem type holds the global list lock while skipping dying instances and gaining passive references, drops the list lock to run the callback only when the shared super lock succeeds, and defers release of the previous reference until after reacquiring the list lock.
Superblock teardown from read copy update context only initializes deferred work and schedules it for process context rather than freeing synchronously.
Superblock wait wake up condition is defined as the combination of born, dying and dead lifecycle states.
Superblock iteration options use the lowest three bits with exclusive on the first, unlocked on the second and reverse on the third.
Freeze level writer tracking uses three ordered labels for normal writers, page fault writers and internal writers.
